**The question.** Which of the string's steps carry over to other instruments, and what changes?

[The series in one paragraph](../instruments-as-operators/index.qmd#the-series-in-one-paragraph)

::: {.newidea}
**In one sentence.** The other instruments run the string's recipe with other numbers: most struck and plucked ones sound at the frequencies of their own eigenvalues, wherever those fall; bowed and blown ones, and the theremin, repeat one cycle, so their partials sit exactly on the whole-number lines.
:::

## The orchestra {#orchestra}

Musicologists sort instruments into five classes by what makes the sound, the [Hornbostel–Sachs](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#hornbostel-sachs) classes: strings, air, solid bodies, stretched skins and electric circuits. Here is one of each, playing Grieg; every voice is built from the spectra on this page.

```{=html}
<p><b>The cards, as text.</b> <i>Where the stems come from.</i> Musicologists sort instruments into five classes by what makes the sound (Hornbostel and Sachs, 1914; electrophones added later). One recipe turns each into its stems. (1) For small motions, Newton's law on a small piece of the instrument takes the form u<sub>tt</sub> = −Au: u is the instrument's shape, and the operator A turns a shape into minus the acceleration it causes. (2) A shape that the operator only stretches, AX = λX, swings at one frequency, f = √λ / 2π. (3) Left to ring, every motion is a sum of such shapes (for a bounded object without friction; post 2 proves it for the string, and the paragraph below gives the theorem for the others), so the list of the λ's, the spectrum of the operator, decides where the stems stand.</p>
<p><i>Electrophone, sine theremin.</i> Kirchhoff's law on a coil and a capacitor; operator A = 1/LC, a single number, like a mass on a spring; spectrum f = 1/(2π√(LC)). One stem: a pure tone. A real theremin runs two such circuits at radio frequencies, the hand changing C of one, and you hear the difference of their frequencies, with a few overtones.</p>
<p><i>Chordophone, piano.</i> Newton's law on a short piece of stiff steel wire; operator A = −c² d²/dx² + κ² d⁴/dx⁴, ends pinned; spectrum f<sub>n</sub> = n f<sub>0</sub> √(1 + Bn²). Just above the lines, more so as n grows: a note, slightly stretched.</p>
<p><i>Aerophone, clarinet.</i> Newton's law on a thin slice of the air in the tube; operator A = −c² d²/dx² on pressure, closed at the reed and open at the far end; the tube's spectrum f<sub>n</sub> = (2n − 1) c / 4L. Blown, the air repeats one cycle, so the partials sit exactly on the lines; the tube's odd modes make the odd ones strong and the even ones weak: a hollow note.</p>
<p><i>Idiophone, glockenspiel.</i> Newton's law on a thin slice of a steel bar; operator A = κ² d⁴/dx⁴, both ends free; spectrum from cos βL cosh βL = 1, ratios 1 : 2.76 : 5.40. Off the lines, but the overtones die fast: a bright, clean note.</p>
<p><i>Membranophones, bass drum and timpani.</i> Newton's law on a small patch of the drumhead; operator A = −c²Δ, rim held still; spectrum from J<sub>m</sub>(ka) = 0, ratios 1 : 1.59 : 2.14 : 2.30 …; the timpani's spectrum is measured, not derived. Bass drum: struck off centre, mostly round modes, off the lines and fading fast: a boom with no clear pitch. Timpani: the same skin; the air it drags along pulls its spoke modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5, the stroke favours them and the round modes fade fast: a note.</p>
<p><i>Every sound in this video was built from pure tones at these spectra. No recordings, no samples.</i> Made in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic's AI model.</p>
</details></div>
```

Every instrument below is a problem of the same shape as the string's: an equation, how the object is held (its [boundary conditions](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#boundary-condition)), and how it starts or how the player drives it. For the ringing ones, the [theorem of post 2](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#completeness) holds in the same form: each of these operators is [self-adjoint](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#self-adjoint) and $\geq 0$ on a bounded object with a reasonable edge (precisely, it has a [compact resolvent](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#compact-resolvent)), so it has an [orthonormal basis](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#orthonormal) of [eigenfunctions](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#eigenfunction), drifts ($\lambda = 0$) split off (Sturm–Liouville for strings and tubes; a compact [Green's operator](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#green) for bars; Rellich for drums; Courant–Hilbert, vol. 1). A drift is a shape with $\lambda = 0$, which moves as $a + bt$ instead of swinging. The kettledrum is the exception: its radiation, sound carried away into the unbounded air around it, takes it outside this theorem, and its full air loading is beyond this page, which is why its ratios are measured. The air's added mass alone would not (the drums entry's toy model of the air stays inside). Each of the others runs post 2's recipe with its own eigenfunctions and eigenvalues, and with frequencies $f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi$.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The three names in the theorem <span class="needs">uses Hilbert spaces</span></summary>

A *Sturm–Liouville problem* is $-(p\,X')' + q\,X = \lambda\,w\,X$ on a bounded interval, with $p, w > 0$ and one condition at each end of the form $\alpha X + \beta X' = 0$; the string ($p = c^2$, $q = 0$, $w = 1$) and the tubes, open or closed at each end, are of this form, and its eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis (Courant and Hilbert, vol. 1, chapters V and VI). For a bar, $(A + 1)^{-1}$ is an integral operator with a kernel continuous on $[0, L]^2$, the Green's operator, which is compact and self-adjoint, so the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators applies to it, and its eigenfunctions are $A$'s. For a drumhead, Rellich's theorem says that on a bounded region, every sequence of shapes that vanish on the rim and have $\iint u^2$ and $\iint |\nabla u|^2$ bounded has a subsequence converging in mean square; this makes $(A + 1)^{-1}$ compact (Evans, section 5.7). A drift occurs only when $A$ has the eigenvalue 0: on this page, for the glockenspiel bar.

</details>
:::

## Two kinds of entry {#two-kinds}

The entries come in two kinds. A *ringing* entry is struck or plucked, then left alone: it moves as a sum of its modes, each swinging at its own $f_n$ and fading at its own rate, so its sound has partials wherever its spectrum falls. A *self-sustained* entry is fed by the player for as long as the note lasts, through a push that depends on the motion itself, and not in proportion to it: a bow, an air jet, a reed or an amplifier. Its motion settles into one repeating cycle, a [self-sustained oscillation](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#self-sustained).

So a self-sustained entry has two spectra. The *resonator's spectrum* is that of the part being driven, the string, the air column, the reed or the circuit: the eigenvalues of its operator, the frequencies at which it would ring if struck. The *sound's spectrum* is that of one repeating cycle at a playing frequency near a resonance, so its partials are exact whole-number multiples ([post 1](../what-you-hear/index.qmd#why-whole-numbers-repeat)); the drive's waveform and the [resonator](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#resonator) (for the violin, also the body) decide which are strong.

Each entry gives its problem, its spectrum, a demo, what you hear, which of post 2's [six conditions](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#conditions) it keeps, and one musical fact. In every demo the stems are the partials of the sound on the pitch ruler, taller when stronger, and in ringing entries they shrink as each partial fades. The picture moves at the same frequencies, slowed down so that one swing of the lowest takes about a second, and enlarged; where its strengths differ from the stems', the caption says why.

## A piano {#piano}

A piano wire is a string and a bar at once: tension pulls it straight, and the steel resists bending. Time starts when the hammer leaves the wire.
$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx} - \kappa^2u_{xxxx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
u = u_{xx} = 0 \ \text{ at } x = 0, L, \\
u(x, 0) = 0, \quad u_t(x, 0) = v_0(x)\text{: the hammer's blow, concentrated near } x = L/8.
\end{gathered}
$$
Here $c^2 = T/\mu$, tension over mass per length; $\kappa^2 = EI/\mu$, with $E$ steel's [Young's modulus](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#youngs-modulus) and $I = \pi d^4/64$ the [second moment of area](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#second-moment) of a wire of diameter $d$. The ends are [pinned](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#pinned): held, free to pivot.

**Spectrum.** Post 2's sines are the eigenfunctions again, with $\lambda_n = c^2k^2 + \kappa^2k^4$, $k = n\pi/L$: same basis, other numbers. So
$$
\begin{gathered}
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, \\
f_0 = \frac{c}{2L}, \qquad B = \frac{\pi^2EI}{TL^2},
\end{gathered}
$$
each partial a little sharp of its line, more so the higher it is (Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 12).

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="piano">

  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The piano note's partials, each a little sharp of its whole-number line"></svg>

Computed: the stem positions, with B = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴, a rough value for a middle C wire. Modelled: each mode starts in proportion to its height under the hammer, with a roll-off for the felt. Illustrative: the fading times.</p>
</div></div>
```

**What you hear.** A clear note whose upper partials run slightly sharp; the player controls the hammer's speed (harder is louder and brighter, as the felt stiffens when squashed), the key's release, which drops a felt damper on the wire, and the pedals, none of which moves a frequency ([A Piano](../a-piano/index.qmd)).

**Post 2's conditions.** All six hold while the key is down. The damper is friction over a short stretch that, unlike post 2's light touch, reaches every mode, so it breaks *no friction, or friction the sines split*; landing at one moment, it also breaks *unchanging in time*.

**Musical fact.** The second partial exceeds twice the fundamental by a factor of about $1 + 3B/2$, so an exact 2 : 1 octave [beats](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#beats); tuners widen octaves, most at the keyboard's ends, a stretch Railsback measured (Railsback 1938).

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from <span class="needs">uses partial derivatives</span></summary>

Take the piece of wire between $x$ and $x + dx$, of mass $\mu\,dx$. Tension gives it the string's net force, $T\,u_{xx}\,dx$ for small slopes ([post 2](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#newton)). Bending gives it the bar's: a bent wire carries the [bending moment](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#moment) $M = EI\,u_{xx}$, the turning balance of each thin slice makes the sideways *shear force* $V = -M_x$, and the shear forces on the two faces differ by $V_x\,dx = -EI\,u_{xxxx}\,dx$ (the kalimba's fold below has the steps). Newton's law takes the total force, so the two add:
$$
\mu\,u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx}.
$$
Small slopes also keep the tension at $T$. At each end the bridge or the bearing point holds the wire in place, $u = 0$, and if it lets the wire pivot freely it exerts no bending moment, $u_{xx} = 0$. The model takes a plain, uniform steel wire; bass strings are wound with copper, which adds mass but little stiffness (Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 12).

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The spectrum, step by step <span class="needs">uses derivatives and square roots</span></summary>

$X = \sin kx$ with $k = n\pi/L$ vanishes at both ends, and so does $X'' = -k^2X$: both pinned conditions hold. Two derivatives multiply it by $-k^2$ and four by $k^4$, so $AX = (c^2k^2 + \kappa^2k^4)X$ with $A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4$: the sines are eigenfunctions, and the string's eigenvalue and the bar's add. There are no others: the sines are already a basis (post 2's theorem), and $A$ is symmetric with these ends, so an eigenfunction for any other eigenvalue would be orthogonal to every sine, hence zero. Factoring, $\lambda_n = c^2k^2(1 + (EI/T)k^2)$, and $f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi$ gives the formula with $B = \pi^2EI/TL^2$. For a middle C wire, roughly $d = 1$ mm and $L = 0.6$ m, steel's $E = 2\times10^{11}$ Pa and density 7850 kg/m³ need a tension of about 610 N, and then $B \approx 4.4\times10^{-4}$: the 10th partial sits $1200\log_2\sqrt{(1 + 100B)/(1 + B)} \approx 37$ [cents](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#cents) sharp of ten times the fundamental. For the octave, $f_2/f_1 = 2\sqrt{(1 + 4B)/(1 + B)} \approx 2(1 + 3B/2)$. These numbers are rough; real strings vary.

</details>
:::

## A kalimba {#kalimba}

A kalimba tine is a steel bar clamped at the bridge and free at its tip, springing back because steel resists bending. The thumb pushes the tip aside a distance $h$ and lets go.
$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2u_{xxxx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
u = u_x = 0 \ \text{ at } x = 0, \\
u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 \ \text{ at } x = L, \\
u(x, 0) = \frac{h\,x^2(3L - x)}{2L^3}, \\ u_t(x, 0) = 0.
\end{gathered}
$$
Here $\kappa^2 = EI/\rho S$, with $\rho$ the density, $S$ the cross-section's area; the base is [clamped](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#clamped), unable to move or tilt, and the tip [free](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#free-end). The start is the smooth cubic a push at the tip bends the tine into; a corner would cost infinite bending energy $\int (u_{xx})^2$. It fails only $u_{xxx}(L) = 0$, where the thumb pushed, which post 2's [weak sense of solution](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#shapes-and-states) allows (fold).

**Spectrum.** $\lambda_n = \kappa^2\beta_n^4$, where $\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1$, so $\beta_nL = 1.8751, 4.6941, 7.8548, \dots$ and $f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi = \kappa\beta_n^2/2\pi$, ratios $1 : 6.27 : 17.55$, off the lines (Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 2).

Computed: the stem positions and each stem's starting height, the push on the bridge (the shear force at the clamp) from the cubic start. Illustrative: the fading times, chosen to match Chapman's observation that the overtones die within a fraction of a second; the stems shrink as each partial fades. The tine is drawn as it moves; in displacement its first overtone is only 2.5% of the fundamental, so the picture shows mostly the first mode, while in the push on the bridge it starts at 55%.</p>

**What you hear.** A click, then a clean note: the first overtone starts strong in the push on the bridge and dies within a fraction of a second, as Chapman observed (the model does not derive it); the player sets the loudness by how far the tip is pushed, and can stop a tine with a finger.

**Post 2's conditions.** All six hold in the model; the fading is measured, not modelled.

**Musical fact.** $\beta_nL$ does not depend on $L$, so $f_1 \propto 1/L^2$: half the length sounds two octaves up, and makers tune a tine by sliding it over the bridge (Kalimba Magic).

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from <span class="needs">uses partial derivatives and an integral over a cross-section</span></summary>

Bend the bar, and fibers on the outside of the curve stretch while those on the inside compress; a middle line, the neutral axis, keeps its length. For small slopes the curvature is $u_{xx}$, and a fiber at height $y$ above the neutral axis is stretched by the fraction $-y\,u_{xx}$, so by Hooke's law it carries the force per unit area $-E\,y\,u_{xx}$. Over the cross-section these forces cancel, but their turning effects add up to the [bending moment](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#moment)
$$
\begin{gathered}
M = -\int y\,(-E\,y\,u_{xx})\,dA = EI\,u_{xx}, \\
I = \int y^2\,dA .
\end{gathered}
$$
Each face of a thin slice also carries a sideways shear force $V$. A thin slice's rotational inertia is negligible, so the turning effects on it balance: $V\,dx + dM = 0$, that is, $V = -M_x = -EI\,u_{xxx}$. The shear forces on the two faces differ by $V_x\,dx$, which accelerates the slice's mass $\rho S\,dx$:
$$
\rho S\,u_{tt} = V_x = -EI\,u_{xxxx},
$$
the [Euler–Bernoulli beam](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#beam) equation, with $\kappa^2 = EI/\rho S$. A fourth-order equation needs two conditions at each end. The clamped base can neither move nor tilt: $u = u_x = 0$. At the free tip nothing bends or pushes the bar: $M = 0$ and $V = 0$, that is, $u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0$. The model ignores the slices' rotational inertia and shear deformation, which matter only for thick bars and high modes (Wikipedia, Euler–Bernoulli beam theory).

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The spectrum, step by step <span class="needs">uses a 2×2 determinant</span></summary>

With $\lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4$ the mode equation is $X'''' = \beta^4X$, solved by $\cos\beta x$, $\sin\beta x$, $\cosh\beta x$ and $\sinh\beta x$, where $\cosh y = (e^y + e^{-y})/2$ and $\sinh y = (e^y - e^{-y})/2$ are the [hyperbolic functions](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#hyperbolic). The clamp, $X(0) = X'(0) = 0$, leaves
$$
\begin{aligned}
X = {} & a\,(\cos\beta x - \cosh\beta x) \\
& + b\,(\sin\beta x - \sinh\beta x).
\end{aligned}
$$
With $c_1 = \cos\beta L$, $s_1 = \sin\beta L$, $c_2 = \cosh\beta L$, $s_2 = \sinh\beta L$, the free tip's $X''(L) = X'''(L) = 0$ reads $-(c_1 + c_2)a - (s_1 + s_2)b = 0$ and $(s_1 - s_2)a - (c_1 + c_2)b = 0$. A solution other than $a = b = 0$ exists exactly when the [determinant](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#determinant) vanishes:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& (c_1 + c_2)^2 + (s_1 + s_2)(s_1 - s_2) \\
& \quad = 2 + 2c_1c_2 = 0,
\end{aligned}
$$
using $c_1^2 + s_1^2 = 1$ and $c_2^2 - s_2^2 = 1$. So $\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1$. Since $\cosh\beta L$ grows fast, $\cos\beta L$ must be near 0, so $\beta_nL$ is near $(n - \tfrac12)\pi$; numerically $1.8751, 4.6941, 7.8548, 10.9955$. Pinned ends would give the sines and the ratios $1 : 4 : 9$; the clamp and the free tip shift the first root most, which puts the ratios off the lines.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>The cubic start, and how much of each mode it holds <span class="needs">uses integration by parts</span></summary>

Before release, a push $F$ at the tip holds the tine still. Inside, nothing pushes, so $EI\,u_0'''' = 0$: $u_0$ is a cubic. The clamp gives $u_0(0) = u_0'(0) = 0$, the free tip carries no moment, $u_0''(L) = 0$, and the tip height is $h$: this leaves $u_0 = h\,x^2(3L - x)/2L^3$, smooth, with $u_0'''(L) = -3h/L^3 \neq 0$, the shear force $F = 3EIh/L^3$ of the thumb. Any shape with a corner has $u_x$ jumping, so $u_{xx}$ contains a spike and the bending energy $\tfrac12 EI\int(u_{xx})^2$ is infinite; a finite push cannot store infinite energy. In post 2's definition a solution is tested only against smooth shapes $\varphi$ in the operator's domain, through $\langle u(t), \varphi\rangle$, so the series of post 2 needs only a start of finite bending energy with $u_0 = u_0' = 0$ at the clamp; the tip's natural conditions need not hold. Its coordinates: with the modes $X_n$ scaled so that $\int_0^L X_n^2 = L$, integrating by parts four times gives $\rho SL\,\omega_n^2\,a_n = F\,X_n(L)$, and $X_n(L) = \pm 2$ for every $n$, so $a_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2$ and $a_2/a_1 = 1/6.27^2 \approx 2.5\%$. The bridge feels the shear force at the clamp, $EI\,u_{xxx}(0)$, in which mode $n$ carries the extra factor $X_n'''(0) \propto \sigma_n\beta_n^3$ ($\sigma_1 = 0.734$, $\sigma_2 = 1.018$): there the second mode starts at about 55% of the first. Chapman measured one dominant overtone at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental on a real kalimba, near the ideal 6.27, dying away quickly after the attack.

</details>
:::

## A glockenspiel {#glockenspiel}

A glockenspiel bar is the same kind of steel bar with both ends free; it rests on soft supports and is struck with a mallet.
$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2u_{xxxx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 \ \text{ at } x = 0 \text{ and } x = L, \\
u(x, 0) = 0, \qquad u_t(x, 0) = v_0(x).
\end{gathered}
$$
Here $\kappa^2 = EI/\rho S$ as for the kalimba, and $v_0$ is the mallet's blow, concentrated where it lands.

**Spectrum.** Two eigenvalues are 0: the bar sliding ($X = 1$) or tilting ($X = x$) without bending, two drifts, which make no sound. The others are $\lambda_n = \kappa^2\beta_n^4$ with $\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = 1$, so $\beta_nL = 4.7300, 7.8532, 10.9956, \dots$ and $f_n = \kappa\beta_n^2/2\pi$, in the ratios $1 : 2.756 : 5.404$, off the lines (Fletcher and Rossing, chapters 2 and 19).

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="glockenspiel">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A glockenspiel bar on two supports, swinging in its first three modes"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The bar's partials at 1, 2.76 and 5.40 times its lowest frequency, off the whole-number lines"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">A bar tuned to C6, 1047 Hz, struck a little off its middle. Computed: the stem positions. Illustrative: the starting strengths and the fading times. The bar is drawn on its two supports, at its fundamental's still points.</p>
</div></div>
```

**What you hear.** A bright, clear note: the overtones sit off the lines, but they are high and die quickly, leaving the fundamental (UBC PHYS 341 wiki, after Fletcher and Rossing); the player sets the loudness by the strength of the blow, the brightness by the mallet (brass or hard plastic is brighter than rubber or yarn), and, by where the mallet lands, how strongly each mode starts; an orchestral glockenspiel often has no dampers, so players stop the ring with a hand.

**Post 2's conditions.** $A$ is only $\geq 0$: the drifts break *$A$ is positive*. The supports hold them: the bar rests at its fundamental's two still points, $0.224L$ from each end, so they barely damp the fundamental.

**Musical fact.** Xylophone and marimba bars are thinned underneath to put their first overtone on a whole-number line, 3× on a xylophone and 4× on a marimba; glockenspiel bars are left uniform (Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 19; UBC PHYS 341 wiki).

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from</summary>

It is the kalimba tine's beam equation, from the same slice of bar (fold above). Only the ends differ: on soft supports both ends are free, so at each end no bending moment and no shear force act, $u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0$. The supports are taken as not holding the bar at all; resting at the fundamental's still points, they are where that mode does not move.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The spectrum, step by step <span class="needs">uses a 2×2 determinant</span></summary>

With $\lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4$, $X = b_1\cos\beta x + b_2\sin\beta x + b_3\cosh\beta x + b_4\sinh\beta x$. The free left end, $X''(0) = X'''(0) = 0$, gives $b_3 = b_1$ and $b_4 = b_2$. With $c_1, s_1, c_2, s_2$ as in the kalimba's fold, the free right end gives $(c_2 - c_1)b_1 + (s_2 - s_1)b_2 = 0$ and $(s_2 + s_1)b_1 + (c_2 - c_1)b_2 = 0$, whose determinant is $(c_2 - c_1)^2 - (s_2^2 - s_1^2) = 2 - 2c_1c_2$. So $\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = 1$, with roots $\beta L = 4.7300, 7.8532, 10.9956, \dots$ For $\lambda = 0$, $X'''' = 0$ with free ends leaves exactly $X = a + bx$: two eigenfunctions with eigenvalue 0, whose coordinates move as $q = a + bt$. The fundamental's still points, where $X_1 = 0$, are at $0.224L$ and $0.776L$ (computed).

</details>
:::

## Drums {#drums}

A drumhead is a sheet pulled tight, a string with a second dimension. The bass drum and the kettledrum, one of the timpani, share this entry.
$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = c^2\,\Delta u \ \text{ on the disk } r < a, \\
u = 0 \ \text{ on the rim } r = a, \\
u(\cdot, 0) = 0, \qquad u_t(\cdot, 0) = v_0 .
\end{gathered}
$$
Here $c^2 = T/\sigma$, the tension per unit length of cut over the mass per unit area; $\Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy}$ is the [Laplacian](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#laplacian); and $v_0$ is the stick's blow, concentrated near the strike point.

**Spectrum.** $\lambda_{m,n} = c^2j_{m,n}^2/a^2$, where $j_{m,n}$ is the $n$-th positive zero of the [Bessel function](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#bessel) $J_m$; the mode $J_m(j_{m,n}r/a)\cos m\theta$ has $m$ still lines through the center and $n - 1$ still circles inside the rim. So $f_{m,n} = c\,j_{m,n}/2\pi a$, in the ratios $1 : 1.593 : 2.136 : 2.295 : 2.653 : 2.917 : \cdots$, between the lines (Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 3).

Step through what separates the two drums: where each is struck, what surrounds its head, and which modes fade first.

**What you hear.** The bass drum booms: struck slightly off center, it starts mostly round modes, off the lines and fading fast, and the player shortens it by muffling the head with a leg or a towel (Aleo; Graham). The kettledrum plays a note: the air its head drags along pulls the spoke modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 times a base, the timpanist strikes between halfway and three-quarters of the way out, where the lowest round mode starts more weakly than the spoke modes, and the round modes radiate their energy away within a fraction of a second (HyperPhysics; Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 18); the timpanist retunes it with a pedal that changes the head's tension.

**Post 2's conditions.** The ideal head keeps all six. The kettledrum breaks post 2's symmetry condition, here through the air around the head rather than at the ends: sound carried away into the unbounded air makes its problem non-self-adjoint (the air's added mass alone would keep it symmetric), and its ratios here are measured.

**Musical fact.** The kettledrum's note is named at the (1,1) mode, its principal tone, and the modes above sit a fifth, an octave and a major tenth higher, the ratios 3/2, 2 and 5/2 (HyperPhysics; Institute of Musical Acoustics, Vienna). A bass drum has a head at each end, commonly tuned about a fourth apart (HyperPhysics).

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from <span class="needs">uses integrals over an area and the divergence theorem</span></summary>

Let $\sigma$ be the head's mass per unit area. A small patch $D$ has mass $\iint_D\sigma\,dA$, so Newton's law for its up-and-down motion reads $\iint_D\sigma\,u_{tt}\,dA$ = the net upward force. A drumhead is a [membrane](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#membrane): a sheet with no stiffness of its own, stretched with the same tension $T$ in every direction, so across each short piece $ds$ of the patch's edge the sheet outside pulls with the force $T\,ds$, along the surface and outward. For small slopes the upward part of that pull is $T$ times the slope outward across the edge, $T\,\partial_nu\,ds$. Adding these around the edge turns, by the [divergence theorem](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#divergence-theorem), into adding $T\,\Delta u$ over the patch:
$$
T\oint_{\partial D}\partial_nu\,ds = T\iint_D\Delta u\,dA .
$$
This holds for every patch, however small, so $\sigma\,u_{tt} = T\,\Delta u$ at every point. In one dimension the same step is $u_x(b) - u_x(a) = \int_a^b u_{xx}\,dx$, the string's. The rim is clamped to the shell: $u = 0$ there. The model leaves out bending stiffness, damping and the air on both sides of the head.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The spectrum, step by step <span class="needs">uses polar coordinates</span></summary>

Write $\lambda = c^2k^2$, so a mode satisfies $-\Delta X = k^2X$ with $X = 0$ on the rim. In polar coordinates $\Delta X = X_{rr} + X_r/r + X_{\theta\theta}/r^2$ ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_operator#Two_dimensions)). Substituting $X = R(r)\Theta(\theta)$ and multiplying by $r^2/R\Theta$ separates the equation, a [separation of variables](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#separation-of-variables): $(r^2R'' + rR' + k^2r^2R)/R = -\Theta''/\Theta$, the left side depending only on $r$ and the right only on $\theta$, so both equal one constant. Going once around must bring $\Theta$ back to itself, so $\Theta = \cos m\theta$ or $\sin m\theta$ with $m = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, and the constant is $m^2$. Then $r^2R'' + rR' + (k^2r^2 - m^2)R = 0$, Bessel's equation, whose solution finite at the center is $J_m(kr)$. The rim needs $J_m(ka) = 0$, so $k = j_{m,n}/a$. These are all the modes: expanding any mode in a Fourier series in $\theta$ reduces it to Bessel's equation term by term. Each frequency with $m \ge 1$ belongs to exactly two modes, the cosine and the sine, because Bessel functions of different whole-number orders share no positive zero (Bourget's conjecture, proved by Siegel in 1929).

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>The step-through's toy model <span class="needs">uses integrals over an area</span></summary>

*The strike.* A brief push at the point $p$ gives mode $i$ a starting speed in proportion to $X_i(p)$; divided by $(\iint X_i^2\,dA)^{1/2}$, on a head of radius 1 this weight is 1.09 at the center, 0.73 halfway out and 0.37 three-quarters out for the lowest round mode (0,1), and between 0.74 and 1.19 for the spoke modes (1,1) to (4,1) anywhere from halfway to three-quarters. A concert bass drum is played slightly off center (Graham 2017; Aleo 2023), where the spoke modes move little.

*The air's mass.* Treat the air on both sides as not squeezable, and each mode locally as a ripple of wavenumber $k = j_{m,n}/a$. The air such a ripple moves reaches about $1/k$ from the head on each side, which adds a mass of about $2\rho/k$ per unit area ($\rho \approx 1.2$ kg/m³) to the head's $\sigma$: $\omega^2 = Tk^2/(\sigma + 2\rho/k)$, so coarse shapes slow down most, an [added mass](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#added-mass). With $\sigma \approx 0.26$ kg/m² and $a = 0.33$ m (Packer 1993), $2\rho a/\sigma \approx 3.0$, and the spoke modes (1,1) to (4,1) move from $1 : 1.34 : 1.67 : 1.98$ to $1 : 1.42 : 1.83 : 2.24$, halfway to $1.5 : 2 : 2.5$; a full calculation of the air inside and around the head gets the rest (Christian and others 1984).

*The kettle.* The nearly sealed kettle acts as a spring on the volume the head sweeps, $V = \iint u\,dA$, adding $\tfrac12\eta V^2$ to the stored energy. Every mode with $m \ge 1$ sweeps no volume, since $\int_0^{2\pi}\cos m\theta\,d\theta = 0$, so it keeps its frequency exactly; only the round modes are raised.

*What is left out.* Radiation, which takes the real kettledrum outside the theorem of this page's opening; the bass drum's second head, coupled to the first through the air in the shell; the fading, taken from measurement (Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 18).

</details>
:::

## A violin, bowed {#violin}

A bowed violin string is post 2's string, kept going by the bow.
$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0 .
\end{gathered}
$$
**Drive:** the bow hair's friction carries the string along, then lets it slip back when the string's pull wins: a force that depends on the slipping speed, not in proportion to it. As in post 2, $c^2 = T/\mu$.

**The resonator's spectrum** is post 2's: $\lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2$ and $f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi = nc/2L$, on every line.

**The sound** is one repeating cycle, [Helmholtz motion](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#helmholtz-motion): two straight pieces joined by a corner that races from the nut to the bridge and back once per period, $2L/c$. So the playing frequency is $f_1$, the partials sit at $nf_1$, and partial $n$ pushes the bridge in proportion to $1/n$ (fold); the body changes their heights, not their positions.

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="violin">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A bowed string: two straight pieces joined by a corner that races between the nut and the bridge"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The bowed sound's partials on every whole-number line, with the string's own frequencies marked under the axis, also on every line"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">Helmholtz motion of an open G string, 196 Hz. Stems: the sound's partials, computed for the ideal string, with strength 1/n, without the wooden body. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the string's modes, on every line too. The picture is the sum of the first 40 modes; dashed, the corner's path, two arcs of a parabola.</p>
</div></div>
```

**What you hear.** A held note at $f_1$; the left hand chooses $L$ by stopping the string, and adds vibrato; the bow's speed and its distance from the bridge set the loudness, the bow's force and nearness to the bridge the brightness, and the stroke the length (Wolfe).

**Post 2's conditions.** The string keeps all six; the bow breaks *linear* and feeds energy in.

**Musical fact.** Helmholtz watched this motion through a vibration microscope by 1860. The model's cycle repeats exactly; Wolfe calls a real bowed string "nearly exactly periodic", and the bow locks the partials onto the lines although a real string's own modes run slightly sharp (Helmholtz 1860; Wolfe).

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from</summary>

Post 2 derives it ([section 2](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#newton)): on a short piece of string under tension $T$, the upward part of each end's pull is $T$ times the slope for small slopes, so the net force is $T\,u_{xx}\,dx$ and $\mu\,u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx}$; the nut and the bridge hold the ends still, $u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0$. The bow adds a force at one point, which depends on the motion there; how bow and string lock together is observed and modelled numerically (McIntyre, Schumacher and Woodhouse 1983), and this page does not derive it.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Helmholtz motion as a sum of modes <span class="needs">uses the plucked-string formula of post 2</span></summary>

A vibration microscope's lens rides on a vibrating tuning fork, so that a bright speck on the string traces a pattern revealing its motion. With one, Helmholtz saw that at each moment the string is two straight pieces, like a plucked string, with the corner at $x_c$. He showed that the corner's height is proportional to $x_c(L - x_c)$, so it traces two arcs of a parabola, and that the corner moves at the wave speed $c = 2Lf_1$. Put that height in place of the pluck's height $h$ in post 2's coefficients $B_n \propto h\sin(n\pi x_c/L)/(n^2x_c(L - x_c))$: the factor $x_c(L - x_c)$ cancels, leaving $\sin(n\pi x_c/L)/n^2$, and with $x_c = 2Lf_1t$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
u(x, t) = {} & \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{a}{n^2}\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L} \\
& \times \sin(2\pi nf_1t)
\end{aligned}
$$
for some overall size $a$ (on the way back, $L < x_c < 2L$, the same formula describes a corner at $2L - x_c$ with negative height). The motion repeats exactly every $1/f_1$ seconds. The force on the bridge is $T$ times the slope there, and the slope of $\sin(n\pi x/L)$ carries the factor $n\pi/L$, so partial $n$ pushes the bridge in proportion to $1/n$.

</details>
:::

## A flute {#flute}

A flute is a tube of air open at both ends, blown by a jet of air across the embouchure hole near one end, with no reed.
$$
\begin{gathered}
p_{tt} = c^2p_{xx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
p(0, t) = p(L, t) = 0 .
\end{gathered}
$$
**Drive:** the jet, which the air's own back-and-forth motion at the hole swings into and out of the tube, adding air in step with the oscillation (Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 16). Here $p$ is the pressure minus room pressure and $c = \sqrt{K/\rho} \approx 343$ m/s the speed of sound ($K$ the air's [bulk modulus](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#bulk-modulus), $\rho$ its density); an open end holds room pressure, up to a small [end correction](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#end-correction).

**The resonator's spectrum** has the string's numbers: $\lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2$ and $f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi = nc/2L$, on every line (Wolfe).

**The sound** is one repeating cycle near the sounding mode, with partials at exact whole-number multiples; the jet's waveform and the tube decide which are strong.

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="flute">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="The air in a tube open at both ends, shaded by pressure, with thin slabs of air moving back and forth"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The flute's partials on every whole-number line, with the open tube's own frequencies marked under the axis, also on every line"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">A steady D4, 294 Hz. Stems: the sound's partials, all on the lines; their strengths, 1/n², are an illustrative choice. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the open tube's modes, on every line too. Picture: the air in the tube, darker where the pressure is higher, with thin slabs of air that bunch where it is squeezed.</p>
</div></div>
```

**What you hear.** A steady note; the player chooses $L$ with the keys, the loudness with the breath, and the register with a faster, narrower airstream, which makes the tube jump to its next mode (Wolfe).

**Post 2's conditions.** In this model the air column keeps all six; the jet breaks *linear*.

**Musical fact.** With every hole closed, an ever faster, narrower airstream sounds the tube's modes in turn, 1, 2, 3, 4, … times the lowest: the open tube's spectrum, heard as the harmonic series (Wolfe).

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from <span class="needs">uses partial derivatives, including mixed ones</span></summary>

Let $\xi(x, t)$ be how far the air that normally sits at $x$ has moved along the tube, of cross-section $S$. The slab between $x$ and $x + dx$ has mass $\rho S\,dx$ and is pushed by the pressure difference across it, $S[p(x) - p(x + dx)] \approx -S\,p_x\,dx$, so $\rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x$. Squeezed air pushes back: the slab is stretched by the fraction $\xi_x$, and for small changes its pressure drops in proportion, $p = -K\xi_x$, with $K$ the bulk modulus (about 1.4 times atmospheric pressure, for squeezing too fast for heat to flow). Together, $\xi_{tt} = c^2\xi_{xx}$ with $c^2 = K/\rho$; differentiating in $x$ and multiplying by $-K$ gives $p_{tt} = c^2p_{xx}$. At an open end the air meets the room, so $p = 0$; the air just outside moves with the air inside, so the tube acts slightly longer, by about 0.6 of its radius at each open end, the end correction (Wolfe). The model takes a narrow, frictionless, cylindrical tube.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The spectrum, step by step</summary>

With $\lambda = c^2k^2$, a mode solves $X'' = -k^2X$, so $X = a\cos kx + b\sin kx$. Room pressure at $x = 0$ forces $a = 0$, and at $x = L$ needs $\sin kL = 0$, so $k = n\pi/L$: $\lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2$, $f_n = nc/2L$, the string's spectrum, with modes $\sin(n\pi x/L)$.

</details>
:::

## A clarinet {#clarinet}

A clarinet is a tube of air closed at the reed and open at the bell; the reed is a valve.
$$
\begin{gathered}
p_{tt} = c^2p_{xx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
p_x(0, t) = 0 \ \text{(reed)}, \\ p(L, t) = 0 \ \text{(bell)}.
\end{gathered}
$$
**Drive:** the reed, which opens as the mouthpiece pressure rises and closes as it drops, so the air column controls the flow that feeds it. At the nearly shut reed the air cannot move, so it feels no net push: $p_x = 0$, a [Neumann condition](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#neumann); $p$ and $c$ are the flute's.

**The resonator's spectrum.** $\lambda_n = \big((2n - 1)\pi c/2L\big)^2$ and $f_n = (2n - 1)c/4L$: only odd multiples of $c/4L$, half the flute's $c/2L$ for the same length (Wolfe).

**The sound** is one repeating cycle near a resonance, with partials at every whole-number multiple; in the low register the tube makes the odd ones strong and the even ones weak, not absent (Wolfe).

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="clarinet">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="The air in a tube closed at the reed on the left and open at the bell, shaded by pressure, with thin slabs of air moving back and forth"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The clarinet's partials on every whole-number line, strong odd ones and faint even ones, with the tube's own frequencies marked under the axis on the odd lines only"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">A steady D3, 147 Hz. Stems: the sound's partials, on every line, strong odd and faint even ones; the exact strengths are an illustrative choice after Wolfe's description. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the tube's modes, on the odd lines only. Picture: the air column, closed at the reed on the left, drawn with the odd partials only; the faint even ones are left out of the picture.</p>
</div></div>
```

**What you hear.** A hollow note nearly an octave below a flute of the same length; the fingers choose $L$, the breath the loudness and brightness (harder is brighter), and the register key jumps the tube to its next mode (Wolfe).

**Post 2's conditions.** In this model the air column keeps all six; the reed breaks *linear*.

**Musical fact.** The tube's next mode is 3 times its lowest, so a clarinet overblows a twelfth, an octave and a fifth, where a flute overblows an octave; clarinet fingerings repeat a twelfth apart (Wolfe).

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from</summary>

The flute's derivation (fold above) gives $p_{tt} = c^2p_{xx}$ and $\rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x$. At the reed the opening is nearly shut, so the air there cannot move: $\xi = 0$ at all times, so $\xi_{tt} = 0$, and Newton's law $\rho\,\xi_{tt} = -p_x$ gives $p_x = 0$. The bell is open: $p = 0$. A real clarinet's bore is not exactly cylindrical, and its holes and bell matter; they refine the numbers, not the picture.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The spectrum, step by step</summary>

With $X = a\cos kx + b\sin kx$, the reed's $X'(0) = bk = 0$ forces $b = 0$, and the bell's $X(L) = 0$ needs $\cos kL = 0$, so $kL = (2n - 1)\pi/2$: one quarter wave, three quarter waves, and so on. So $\lambda_n = \big((2n - 1)\pi c/2L\big)^2$ and $f_n = (2n - 1)c/4L$, with modes $\cos\big((2n - 1)\pi x/2L\big)$.

</details>
:::

## A harmonica {#harmonica}

A harmonica reed is a small brass bar riveted at one end over a slot: the kalimba tine's problem, driven by airflow.
$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2u_{xxxx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
u = u_x = 0 \ \text{ at the rivet}, \\
u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 \ \text{ at the tip}.
\end{gathered}
$$
**Drive:** the airflow through the slot, which the reed opens and shuts as it swings through, a [free reed](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#free-reed). Here $\kappa^2 = Eh^2/12\rho$ for a reed of thickness $h$.

**The resonator's spectrum** is the tine's: $f_n = \kappa\beta_n^2/2\pi$, ratios $1 : 6.27 : 17.55$, off the lines.

**The sound.** The reed settles into one repeating cycle, at a frequency somewhat below its lowest mode's (Cottingham), and lets through one identical puff of air per cycle; the sound comes mainly from the puffs (Pykett). Repeating puffs have partials only at whole-number multiples, odd and even both strong (Pykett), none at 6.27×; each puff's shape, with the player's mouth and the reed chamber, decides which are strong, not the reed's own modes.

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="harmonica">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A reed riveted over its slot, swinging through it and letting out one puff of air per cycle, with a trace of the airflow"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The blown reed's partials on every whole-number line, with the reed's own frequencies marked under the axis at 1 and 6.27 times"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">A C5 reed, 523 Hz, blown. Stems: the sound's partials, at whole-number multiples of the playing frequency, computed from the puff drawn on the right: one puff per cycle, open for about 30% of it, a shape chosen for illustration. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the reed's modes, at 1 and 6.27 times its lowest; the playing frequency sits somewhat below the lowest, drawn here at 1. The reed is drawn in its first mode, and the slot is drawn open only while the tip is above the plate.</p>
</div></div>
```

**What you hear.** A steady note on the lines; the breath sets the loudness and, through each puff's shape, the tone, while the pitch hardly moves (Pykett).

**Post 2's conditions.** The reed keeps all six; the valve breaks *linear*.

**Musical fact.** Players bend notes down on a diatonic harmonica by reshaping mouth and throat; the bent note lies between the hole's two notes, because the hole's blow and draw reeds, over one chamber, both take part (Bahnson, Antaki and Beery 1998).

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from</summary>

It is the kalimba tine's beam equation (fold in the kalimba entry), for brass: clamped at the rivet, $u = u_x = 0$, and free at the tip, $u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0$. For a rectangular reed of width $w$ and thickness $h$, $I = wh^3/12$ and $S = wh$, so $\kappa^2 = EI/\rho S = Eh^2/12\rho$, and $f_1 = (1.8751)^2\,h\sqrt{E/12\rho}/(2\pi L^2)$: the width cancels.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Why a repeating airflow has only whole-number partials, and how the demo makes its sound</summary>

Let $q(t)$ be the airflow through the slot. In the steady oscillation it repeats every $P = 1/f_p$ seconds, $q(t + P) = q(t)$, so its [Fourier series](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#fourier-series) contains only $\cos(2\pi nt/P)$ and $\sin(2\pi nt/P)$: frequencies $nf_p$ ([post 1](../what-you-hear/index.qmd#why-whole-numbers-repeat)). The argument uses only that the motion repeats, not which modes make it up. That the reed locks into one repeating motion is observed, and reproduced by nonlinear models of reeds, but not derived here; a plausible picture is that the airflow feeds mainly the first mode, and the others move only as they are pushed, at multiples of $f_p$. The demo's puff is $q = \max(0, \sin 2\pi f_pt - 0.6)$, chosen so that the open part of each cycle is short; its Fourier coefficients, with a gentle roll-off, are the stems.

</details>
:::

## A theremin {#theremin}

A theremin makes its tone with electric circuits, each a coil and a capacitor, an [LC circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LC_circuit), whose charge swings like a mass on a spring.
$$
\ddot q = -\frac{1}{LC}\,q .
$$
**Drive:** an amplifier that feeds the circuit in step with its swing and limits it to a steady size. Here $q$ is the charge on the capacitor, $L$ the coil's [inductance](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#inductance) and $C$ the [capacitance](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#capacitance), so $A = 1/LC$, one number.

**The resonator's spectrum.** One eigenvalue, $\lambda = 1/LC$, so one frequency, $f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$, a radio frequency below 500 kHz (Wikipedia, Theremin).

**The sound.** The instrument runs two such circuits, one fixed and one whose capacitance the player's hand changes, and a mixer outputs the difference of their frequencies, in the audible range ([heterodyning](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#heterodyning)). The demo plays a sine theremin: one partial.

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="theremin">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A coil and a capacitor, with the charge sloshing between the capacitor's plates"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="One partial, at 1 times"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">An idealized sine theremin at A4, 440 Hz: one stem. A real theremin's tone has a few overtones. No resonator ticks: the circuits' own frequencies are radio frequencies, far beyond this ruler, and the tone you hear is the difference of two of them. Picture: one coil-and-capacitor circuit, its charge sloshing between the plates, slowed to about one swing a second.</p>
</div></div>
```

**What you hear.** A tone with few overtones, gliding as the hand moves; most players set the pitch with the right hand's distance from one antenna and the loudness with the left hand's distance from the other (Wikipedia, Theremin).

**Post 2's conditions.** The circuit alone keeps all six; the amplifier breaks *linear*, and a moving hand changes $C$ as the circuit swings, breaking *unchanging in time*, like post 2's turned peg.

**Musical fact.** Leon Theremin invented the instrument in 1920 and patented it in 1928; it is played without being touched (Wikipedia, Theremin).

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from</summary>

Kirchhoff's voltage law, which balances voltages as Newton's law balances forces, says that the voltages around a closed loop add to zero. A capacitor holding charge $q$ has the voltage $q/C$ across it; a coil carrying the current $I = \dot q$ has the voltage $L\,\dot I$. Around the loop, $L\,\ddot q + q/C = 0$, that is, $\ddot q = -q/LC$: the coil plays the mass and $1/C$ the spring's stiffness. For ideal parts both laws are linear, so no small-motion step is needed.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>How two radio frequencies make one audible tone</summary>

A mixer multiplies the two oscillators' signals, and $\sin(2\pi f_1t)\sin(2\pi f_2t) = \tfrac12\cos(2\pi(f_1 - f_2)t) - \tfrac12\cos(2\pi(f_1 + f_2)t)$; a filter keeps the difference. With both near a few hundred kilohertz, a hand that changes one circuit's capacitance by a small fraction moves the difference across the whole audible range. Real theremins' mixers and circuits add a few overtones, on the whole-number lines of the difference frequency, since the output repeats at that rate.

</details>
:::

## What we found

Every instrument here runs post 2's recipe: an equation, how the object is held, and a start or a drive. Struck and plucked, the piano, the kalimba, the glockenspiel and the bass drum sound at the frequencies of their own eigenvalues, a little sharp of the lines, far off them, or scattered between them, while the kettledrum's air pulls one set near the lines. Bowed and blown, the violin, the flute, the clarinet and the harmonica repeat one cycle, and so does the theremin's output, at the difference frequency, so their partials sit exactly on the lines, and the drive and the resonator decide only which are strong.

```{=html}
<script src="orchestra.js"></script>
<script>
// The orchestra: one instrument from each Hornbostel–Sachs class, drawn and played by orchestra.js.
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var O = window.Orchestra; if (!O) return;
  // On this page each family's card points to its entry below.
  var HERE = { electro: "The theremin: entry below", chord: "The piano: entry below", aero: "The clarinet: entry below", idio: "The glockenspiel: entry below", membrane: "The two drums: entry below" };
  O.FAM.forEach(function (f) { if (HERE[f.id]) f.where = HERE[f.id]; });
  var fams = document.getElementById("oFams"), mute = {};

    b.style.setProperty("--c", "rgb(" + f.hue.join(",") + ")"); b.innerHTML = '<span class="dot"></span>' + f.inst;
    b.addEventListener("click", function () { mute[f.id] = !mute[f.id]; b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", mute[f.id] ? "false" : "true"); applyMute(f.id); if (!ctx) drawRest(); });
    fams.appendChild(b);

  }

  document.getElementById("oFull").addEventListener("click", function () { play(true); });
  document.getElementById("oStop").addEventListener("click", stop);
  var fsb = document.getElementById("oFs");
  if (!cv.requestFullscreen) fsb.hidden = true;
  fsb.addEventListener("click", function () { if (cv.requestFullscreen) cv.requestFullscreen().catch(function () {}); });
  document.addEventListener("fullscreenchange", function () { fit(); if (!ctx) drawRest(); });
  window.addEventListener("resize", function () { fit(); if (!ctx) drawRest(); });

  if (document.fonts && document.fonts.load) Promise.all(faces.map(function (f) { return document.fonts.load(f, "A−κ♯"); })).then(function () { if (!ctx) drawRest(); }, function () {});
})();
</script>
```
